title: Words & Language · Episode 2
chapters: The people who wrote the dictionary

units.t: Words & Language. Episode two.
In this episode: How Australian English was born, Where words come from, The people who wrote the dictionary and The world's languages.
Part one. How Australian English was born.
Within a generation of 1788, visitors noticed that children in the colony sounded different.
Here is how a new way of speaking English took shape.
A new accent, quickly.
The First Fleet that arrived in 1788 carried people from all over Britain and Ireland: Londoners, rural English, Irish convicts, Scots and more.
Their parents spoke a jumble of dialects.
But children growing up together in Sydney did what children everywhere do: they copied each other more than their parents.
By the 1820s, visitors were already remarking that native born children, sometimes called currency lads and lasses, spoke differently.
Linguists call this dialect levelling.
When many accents mix, the strongest regional quirks tend to drop out and a new shared accent emerges.
That is why Australian English is fairly uniform across a huge continent.
Words from Aboriginal languages.
When Captain Cook's expedition was stranded near what is now Cooktown in 1770, the crew recorded a word that sounded like 'kangaroo' from the local Guugu Yimithirr people.
It became one of the most famous loanwords in the world.
After 1788, settlers in Sydney borrowed more words from the Dharug language, including 'dingo', 'wombat' and 'koala'.
'Boomerang' also came from a Sydney area language, and 'billabong' is thought to come from Wiradjuri.
Hundreds of Australian place names, from Wagga Wagga to Kakadu, have Aboriginal origins too.
Before colonisation there were around 250 Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages, many with several dialects.
Many are now endangered, and communities are working to revive them.
Arvo, servo and brekkie.
Ask an Aussie what they did this arvo and you might hear that they stopped at the servo, grabbed a sanga and caught up with a rello.
Australian English is famous for diminutives: shortened words with an ending added.
The two big endings are 'ie' or 'y', as in 'brekkie', 'barbie' and 'sunnies', and 'o', as in 'arvo', 'ambo', 'smoko' and 'bottle-o'.
There are a great many of these forms.
Despite the stereotype, they are not about laziness.
Research suggests they often signal friendliness, informality and shared identity.
Notice how 'ambo' sounds warmer than 'paramedic'.
Fair dinkum and accents.
'Dinkum' appears in English regional speech in the 1800s, where it seems to have meant work or a fair share of work.
In Australia it came to mean genuine, and 'fair dinkum' became a catchphrase.
A popular story says it comes from Chinese miners saying 'ding kum' for real gold, but there is no good evidence for this.
In the 1960s, linguists Alexander Mitchell and Arthur Delbridge recorded thousands of school students and described three broad accent types.
'Broad' is the stereotypical outback sound, heard in the voice of Steve Irwin.
'Cultivated' is closer to British pronunciation and was once common among radio announcers.
'General', in between, is what most Australians speak.
These are points on a scale, and cultivated has become much rarer.
Bathers, togs and myths.
Accents are fairly uniform, but vocabulary is another story.
What you wear to the beach depends on your state: 'bathers' is common in Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia, 'togs' in Queensland, and 'swimmers' or 'cossie' in New South Wales.
A slice of fried potato in batter is a 'potato cake' in Melbourne and a 'potato scallop' in Sydney.
Processed sandwich meat is 'devon', 'fritz', 'polony' or 'Belgium sausage' depending on where you grew up.
An old myth says Australians speak with half closed mouths to keep out flies, or that the accent comes from lazy or drunk convicts.
Linguists reject this.
Every accent is the result of speech drifting over time.
Australian English sits alongside British, American and Indian English as a major variety.
A humorous 1965 book, Let Stalk Strine, popularised the jokey name 'Strine'.
The key idea: The Australian accent formed surprisingly quickly among the first colonial children.
Part two. Where words come from.
'Nice' once meant foolish, 'silly' once meant blessed, and 'muscle' means little mouse.
Every word has a backstory, and the true ones are often stranger than the myths.
Words have histories.
Etymology, from Greek words meaning 'the study of true meaning', traces words back through time by comparing old manuscripts, dictionaries and related languages.
The Oxford English Dictionary, begun in 1857 and completed in 1928, pioneered printing dated quotations showing each word's earliest known uses.
A word's origin doesn't fix its meaning today, but it often explains odd spellings and hidden connections.
Meanings rarely stay still.
'Nice' comes from Latin nescius, ignorant, and in Middle English meant foolish before drifting through 'fussy' and 'precise' to 'pleasant'.
'Silly' went the other way: Old English sælig meant happy or blessed, then innocent, pitiable, then foolish.
'Awful' once meant inspiring awe.
Linguists call these shifts amelioration and pejoration.
Hidden pictures.
Plenty of words hide little pictures.
'Muscle' comes from Latin musculus, 'little mouse', perhaps because a flexing muscle looked like a mouse moving under the skin.
'Disaster' comes via Italian from 'bad star', reflecting an old belief that the planets shaped events.
'Daisy' comes from Old English dæges ēage, 'day's eye', because the flower opens at dawn and closes at dusk.
'Clue' was once 'clew', a ball of thread, like the one Theseus used to escape the labyrinth.
'Robot' comes from Czech robota, forced labour, popularised by Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.
U.
R.
An apron was a napron.
Sometimes words change because of how we split up speech.
In Middle English, 'a napron' was heard as 'an apron', and the 'n' slid across; a related form with the 'n' survives in 'napkin'.
'A nadder' became 'an adder', and 'a noumpere' became 'an umpire'.
It can go the other way too: 'an ewt' became 'a newt', and 'an ekename', meaning an additional name, became 'a nickname'.
Linguists call this rebracketing.
It's a reminder that language lives in the ear first and on the page second.
Girl is another surprise: in Middle English it could mean a young person of either sex.
Beware folk etymology.
Catchy word origins spread fast, and many are false.
'Posh' supposedly stands for 'port out, starboard home', the shady cabins on voyages to India, but no tickets stamped this way have ever been found.
There's no evidence that 'rule of thumb' came from a law about beating wives, and 'sincere' doesn't come from sine cera, 'without wax'.
Most words older than the 20th century didn't begin as acronyms.
The claim that Roman soldiers were paid in salt, giving us 'salary', is also unproven, though the word is linked to Latin sal, salt.
Good dictionaries flag uncertain origins.
Aboriginal loanwords.
Australian English has borrowed several hundred words from Aboriginal languages, mostly for animals, plants and places.
Early loans came from the Sydney language, often called Dharug: dingo, wallaby, wombat and koala, from gula.
'Galah' comes from Yuwaalaraay and Gamilaraay, 'yabby' from Wemba Wemba.
Many place names, from Parramatta to Wagga Wagga, are Aboriginal too, though some meanings are disputed.
A popular story says 'kangaroo' means 'I don't understand'.
It's a myth.
In 1770, while the Endeavour was repaired near present-day Cooktown, the crew recorded gangurru from Guugu Yimithirr speakers.
In the 1970s, linguist John Haviland confirmed it names a large kangaroo.
When the word reached Sydney, locals didn't recognise it.
To check origins, use the Macquarie Dictionary or Online Etymology Dictionary, and trust notes saying 'origin uncertain'.
The key idea: Etymology traces how words' forms and meanings have changed, and meanings can drift or even flip.
Part three. The people who wrote the dictionary.
Somebody had to decide what every word means.
Meet the stubborn, eccentric and occasionally imprisoned people who built the English dictionary.
Before dictionaries.
Shakespeare wrote his plays with no dictionary of ordinary English on his desk.
That was normal.
For centuries, English speakers simply used words and argued about them.
The first English dictionaries appeared around 1600 and were modest.
Robert Cawdrey's A Table Alphabeticall, published in 1604, listed only about 2,500 'hard words', mostly borrowed from Latin, French and Greek, for readers who found them puzzling.
Nobody thought ordinary words like 'dog' or 'run' needed defining.
These early books were glossaries for the newly educated, not records of the whole language.
The idea of capturing every word, common or rare, and how it was really used took another century and a half to arrive.
Johnson's dictionary.
In 1746 a group of London booksellers hired Samuel Johnson, a brilliant but often broke writer, to produce a proper dictionary.
The French Academy had taken decades with dozens of scholars.
Johnson, with a handful of assistants in a house off Fleet Street, took about nine years.
His Dictionary of the English Language appeared in 1755 with roughly 42,000 entries.
Its real innovation was evidence.
Johnson read widely, marked passages showing words in action and used more than 100,000 quotations to illustrate meanings.
That method became the foundation of serious dictionary making in English.

A few entries let his wit show, such as 'lexicographer: a writer of dictionaries; a harmless drudge', and his teasing definition of 'oats' as a grain 'which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people'.
Webster's American spelling.
Across the Atlantic, the schoolteacher Noah Webster believed the new United States deserved its own version of English.
He published An American Dictionary of the English Language in 1828 and used it to push spelling changes he thought simpler and more logical.
That is why Americans write 'color', 'center' and 'defense' while Australians, following British habits, write 'colour', 'centre' and 'defence'.
Most of his more radical ideas never caught on, but his choices stuck in schools, newspapers and printing houses.
One determined dictionary maker helped split English spelling into two traditions, which is why spellcheckers ask whether you want Australian or American English.
The Oxford English Dictionary.
In 1857 the Philological Society in London called for a dictionary recording every English word since around the 12th century and how its meaning had changed.
Scottish schoolmaster James Murray became editor in 1879 and worked in a corrugated iron shed, the Scriptorium, lined with pigeonholes for slips of paper.
The first part appeared in 1884, covering only 'A' to 'Ant'.
Murray died in 1915.
The dictionary was finished in 1928, in ten volumes, roughly 70 years after it was proposed.
Murray appealed to the public to post in word examples on slips, and thousands of volunteers in Britain, America and Australia sent millions.
One of the most productive was William Chester Minor, an American former army surgeon confined to Broadmoor, a hospital for the criminally insane, after killing a man in London in 1872.
Dictionaries today.
Australia got its own major dictionary, the Macquarie, in 1981, recording words like 'arvo', 'doona' and 'ute' with Australian meanings and pronunciations.
That reflects a bigger change in thinking.
Early dictionary makers often wanted to fix the language and decide what was correct.
Most modern lexicographers are descriptive instead: they observe how people actually use words and record it, including slang and new coinages.
When a dictionary adds a word, it is not approving it, only noting that enough people use it.
Today editors search huge digital text collections to spot new words and shifting meanings, and online dictionaries are updated several times a year.
Johnson's paper slips have become databases, but the goal is the same.
The key idea: For most of its history, English had no dictionary of everyday words at all.
Part four. The world's languages.
Humans speak around 7,000 languages, yet half of us speak one of just a couple of dozen.
Many of the rest, including most of Australia's own, are at risk of falling silent.
About 7,000 languages.
Linguists count roughly 7,000 living languages, including a few hundred sign languages.

The figure depends on where you draw the line between a language and a dialect, which is often as much about politics as linguistics; a famous quip says 'a language is a dialect with an army and navy'.
Languages are shared very unevenly.
More than half the world's people speak one of only about two dozen, while thousands have fewer than 10,000 speakers each.
English leads in total speakers, roughly 1.
5 billion, followed by Mandarin, Hindi and Spanish.
Mandarin has the most native speakers, then Spanish and English.
Rankings shift with how varieties are grouped, so treat lists as approximate.
Where diversity lives.
Papua New Guinea, with a relatively small population, has around 840 languages, more than any other country and over a tenth of the world's total.
Indonesia and Nigeria each have several hundred.
Rugged mountains, islands, rainforest and a long history of small, independent communities help languages multiply.
Much of Europe has relatively few.
Some languages have features English speakers find astonishing, such as tones that change meaning, or words that pack a whole sentence into one.
Languages in danger.
Around 40% of the world's languages are considered endangered, usually because children are no longer learning them at home.
Pressure comes from bigger languages used in schools, jobs, government and media, and in many places from past policies that punished people for speaking their own language.
When the last speakers die, a language becomes 'sleeping' or extinct, and with it can go knowledge of local plants, animals, history, law and ways of seeing the world.
Estimates of how fast languages are being lost vary, but the trend is clear.
Australia's first languages.
When the British arrived in 1788, Australia was one of the most linguistically diverse places on Earth.
More than 250 distinct languages were spoken, with many dialects.
In the Torres Strait, Meriam Mir and Kala Lagaw Ya are traditional, and the creole Yumplatok is widely spoken.
Across the north, the creole Kriol is the first language of thousands of Aboriginal people.
Colonisation brought dispossession and, for decades, policies that discouraged or banned Aboriginal languages in missions and schools.
The 2020 National Indigenous Languages Report, based on a 2019 survey, found about 120 traditional languages still spoken, but only around 12 learned by children as a first language.
Strong ones include Warlpiri and Pitjantjatjara.
In the 2021 Census, about 77,000 people spoke an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander language at home.
Waking languages up.
Languages no longer spoken are often called 'sleeping', not dead, because they can be woken.
Hebrew, used for centuries mainly in religious study, became an everyday language again from the late 1800s.
Māori language nests, Te Kōhanga Reo, from 1982, and Welsh revival have had real success.
In Australia, Kaurna, the language of the Adelaide Plains, is being revived partly from records made by German missionaries around 1840.
Wiradjuri, Dharug and others are taught in communities, schools and universities.
These languages belong to their communities, who decide how they are shared.
Look for programs run or endorsed by local language centres, learn the name of the Country where you live, and follow community guidance on restricted words, names or songs.
The UN has declared 2022-2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages.
The key idea: There are roughly 7,000 living languages, but half the world's people speak one of about two dozen.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did a distinct Australian accent form so quickly?
Answer. Children copied each other, not their parents' dialects.
Question two. What did 'silly' originally mean in Old English?
Answer. Blessed or happy.
Question three. Why did the first English dictionaries only list 'hard words'?
Answer. Ordinary words seemed too obvious to need explaining.
Question four. About how many living languages are there in the world?
Answer. About 7,000.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
